title: Reading through critical lenses
keyIdea: A critical lens is a set of questions you bring to a text: Marxist critics ask about money, power and work; feminist critics about gender; postcolonial critics about empire; ecocritics about nature; psychoanalytic critics about hidden fears and wishes. One text can support many strong readings, but a reading is only as good as the words that back it, and it is not a claim about what the author intended. Top essays weigh one reading against another.

kid: A critical lens is a set of questions you bring to a text. Each lens makes you notice different things. A Marxist lens asks who has money and power, and who does the work. A feminist lens asks how women and gender roles are shown. A postcolonial lens asks how empire and colonised people are shown.

An ecocritical lens asks how nature is shown and how people treat it. A psychoanalytic lens looks for hidden fears and wishes. Take Blake's poem London from 1794. A Marxist sees the soldier bleeding on the palace walls. An ecocritic sees that even the river is owned.
One text can hold many strong readings. But not anything goes. A good reading points to the words that back it. If no words back it, it is a guess.
A lens is not a claim about what the writer planned. Blake was not reading Marx. You are asking new questions of old words. The best essays weigh one reading against another.
adult: This topic introduces the main critical lenses used at A level and beyond: Marxist, feminist, postcolonial, ecocritical and psychoanalytic. Each is best taught as a set of questions the reader brings, which lets students produce several readings of one text.

The lab uses public-domain texts. Learners match each lens to its question, hunt for the phrase in Blake's London that backs each reading, sort readings of the first line of Pride and Prejudice by whether the words support them, name the lens a critic is using, and build a paragraph in order.

A common mistake is to think a lens reading claims the author's intention, so that a feminist reading of Blake is wrong because he was not a feminist. Another is the belief that there is one right reading, or the opposite, that any reading goes. In fact readings are judged on textual evidence.

Exam boards reward students who consider different interpretations. At home, pick a film you have both seen and ask your teen who has the power in it, and what the story says about women. Then ask which scene proves it.

familyTip: Next time you watch a film together, ask one lens question, such as who has the money and power here, and then ask your teen which scene backs their answer.

practice.prompt: {n} students read London through {n} different lenses, and each backs their reading with quotations. How many readings can be valid?
choices: All {n}, if each is backed by the text
practice.hint: Can a poem support more than one strong reading at the same time?
practice.explain: All {n} can be valid. A text can hold many strong readings, as long as each one is backed by words on the page.

practice.prompt: Your essay has {n} quotations but never makes a claim through a lens. What is missing?
choices: A clear claim about what the lens reveals
practice.hint: Quotations are evidence. Evidence for what?
practice.explain: {n} quotations prove nothing without a claim. Start with what the lens shows you, then use the quotations to back it.

practice.prompt: Which question does a Marxist lens ask?
choices: Who has money and power, and who does the work?
practice.hint: Marxist critics focus on class, money and work.
practice.explain: A Marxist lens asks about money, power, class and work. Nature is the ecocritical question, and hidden fears the psychoanalytic one.

practice.prompt: A critic says Blake's “charter’d Thames” shows a river turned into property. Which lens is that?
practice.hint: Which lens asks how people treat nature?
practice.explain: Ecocritics ask how nature is shown and used. A river being owned is a classic ecocritical point.

practice.prompt: A classmate says your feminist reading of London is wrong because Blake was not a feminist. Best reply?
choices: A lens reading is judged on the text, not on the author's views
You are right, so I will drop it
practice.hint: Is a lens a claim about what the author planned?
practice.explain: A lens is a question you bring to the text. It is judged on the words that back it, not on what Blake believed.

pool.prompt: Which lens asks how empire and colonised people are shown?
pool.hint: Which lens looks at empire, colonies and who tells the story?
pool.explain: Postcolonial critics ask how empire and colonised people are shown, as Edward Said did with Mansfield Park.

pool.prompt: A critic says Elizabeth Bennet's family may lose their home because only a male heir can inherit it. Which lens is that?
pool.hint: Is this point about gender, nature or empire?
pool.explain: Inheritance passing only to men is a point about gender, so it is a feminist reading.

pool.prompt: Your reading of a novel is bold, but you cannot find any words in it that back it up. What should you do?
choices: Change or drop it: a reading needs textual evidence
Keep it: lenses let you say anything
Say the author secretly meant it
pool.hint: What makes a reading strong rather than a guess?
pool.explain: A lens opens new questions, but the answers have to come from the words. With no evidence it is only a guess.

pool.prompt: “Mind-forg’d manacles” in London are chains the mind makes for itself. Which lens fits this reading best?
pool.hint: Which lens looks for hidden fears and the inner mind?
pool.explain: Chains made by the mind point to fears people have taken inside, which is the psychoanalytic question.

pool.prompt: A reading quotes {n} phrases from the poem, and each is really there. A classmate objects that Blake did not intend it. Is that a strong objection?
choices: No: a lens reading stands on textual evidence, not intent
Yes, unless there are more than {n} phrases
pool.hint: Is a lens reading a claim about the author's plan?
pool.explain: With {n} real phrases as evidence, the reading stands. Intent is not the test: the words are.

pool.prompt: An essay spends {n} paragraphs explaining feminist theory, but quotes the novel only once. What is its main weakness?
choices: Too little close reading of the text
It should explain theory for even longer
pool.hint: What do examiners reward: theory or close reading?
pool.explain: {n} paragraphs of theory with one quotation means too little close reading. Use the lens to read the words.

pool.prompt: What lifts a critical essay into the top band?
choices: Weighing your reading against another one
Using every lens in one paragraph
pool.hint: Think about the last move in a strong paragraph.
pool.explain: Top essays develop one reading, then weigh it against an alternative. Piling up lenses or retelling the plot does not.

pool.prompt: In a strong critical paragraph, what comes straight after your claim?
pool.hint: Claim, then what proves it, then analysis.
pool.explain: After the claim comes the quotation that backs it, then analysis of the words, then an alternative reading.

visual.caption: Is each reading of Blake's London backed by the words? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The “Palace walls” show the rulers stained by the soldier's death
The “charter’d Thames” shows nature owned for profit
The “youthful Harlots curse” shows women harmed by poverty
London is a happy poem about a holiday
The poem is set in Paris

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match lenses to their questions, find evidence in Blake's London, test readings of Austen and build a critical paragraph.
